Tischler and Piet Maes The citation for this ICTV Report chapter is the summary published as: Bradfute, S. B., Calisher, C. H., Klempa, B., Klingström, J., Kuhn, J. H., Laenen, L., Tischler, N. D., & Maes, P. (2024). ICTV Virus Taxonomy Profile: Hantaviridae 2024, Journal of General Virology 105, 001975 Corresponding author: Piet Maes ( [email protected] ) Edited by: Holly Hughes and Evelien Adriaenssens Posted: March 2024, updated June 2024 Summary Hantaviridae is a family for negative-sense RNA viruses with genomes of about 10.5–14.6 kb (Table 1 Hantaviridae ). The family includes eight genera ( Actinovirus and Percilovirus (subfamily Actantavirinae ), Agnathovirus (subfamily Agantavirinae ), Loanvirus , Mobatvirus , Orthohantavirus and Thottimvirus (subfamily Mammantavirinae ), and Reptillovirus (subfamily Repantavirinae ). These viruses are maintained in and/or transmitted by small mammals, but also by fish and reptiles. Several orthohantaviruses can infect humans, causing mild, severe, and sometimes-fatal diseases. Hantavirids produce enveloped virions containing three single-stranded RNA segments with open reading frames (ORFs) that encode a nucleoprotein (N), a glycoprotein precursor (GPC), and large (L) protein containing an RNA-directed RNA polymerase (RdRP) domain. Table 1 Hantaviridae. Characteristics of members of the family Hantaviridae. Characteristic Description* Example Hantaan virus (S segment: M14626; M segment: M14627; L segment: X55901), species Orthohantavirus hantanense Virion Enveloped, pleomorphic virions 80–160 nm in diameter with heterodimeric surface spikes Genome Three single-stranded RNA molecules (segments): small (S; 1.0–3.0 kb), medium (M; 3.4–4.8 kb), and large (L; 5.3–6.8 kb) Replication Ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes containing anti-genomic RNA serve as coding templates for synthesis of genomic RNA Translation Proteins are produced from capped and non-polyadenylated mRNAs. The 5′-cap structure is obtained via cap-snatching from cellular mRNAs Host range Fish (actinoviruses, agnathoviruses, perciloviruses), mammals (orthohantaviruses), and reptiles (reptilloviruses) Taxonomy Realm Riboviria , kingdom Orthornavirae , phylum Negarnaviricota , class Bunyaviricetes , order Elliovirales ; the family includes four subfamilies, eight genera, and 55 species * mostly based on experiments with mammalian orthohantaviruses Viruses assigned to each of the seven genera form genus-specifc monophyletic clades based on phylogenetic analysis of concatenated L protein/RdRP, glycoprotein and N sequences. Viruses from all seven genera share one or more of the following characteristics: (i) enveloped pleomorphic virions; (ii) tri-segmented, negative-sense RNA genome without polyadenylated tracts at the 3′-end; (iii) genomic sequence complementarity at the 5′- and 3′-ends; and (iv) capped but not polyadenylated virus mRNAs ( Maes et al., 2004 ). Piscine Hosts Genus Actinovirus . Viruses in this genus infect actinopterygian (percid, ogcocephalid, and triacanthodid, and possibly goblid and melanotaeniid) fish. Genus Agnathovirus . Viruses in this genus infect agnathan (myxinid) fish. Genus Percilovirus . Viruses in this genus infect actinopterygian ( gobiid, lophiid ) fish. Mammalian Hosts Genus Loanvirus. Viruses in this genus infect rhinolophid, verspertillionid, and possibly nycterid bats and possibly murid rodents. Genus Mobatvirus. Viruses in this genus infect emballonurid, hipposiderid, pteropodid and possibly molossid, and vespertillionid bats and soricid and talpid eulipotyphla. Genus Orthohantavirus. Viruses assigned to this genus infect soricid and talpid eulipotyphla and muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents. Genus Thottimvirus. Viruses in this genus infect soricid and possibly talpid eulipotyphla. Reptilian Hosts Genus Reptillovirus . Viruses in this genus infect gekkonid and possibly scincid reptiles. Virion Morphology Only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Physicochemical and physical properties Only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Nucleic acid Hantavirids have tri-segmented, negative-sense RNA genomes (S, M, and L segments). The viral mRNAs are not polyadenylated and contain a 5′-methylated cap and several non-templated nucleotides at the 5′-end that are derived from host cell mRNAs via cap snatching ( Schmaljohn et al., 1985 , Jonsson and Schmaljohn 2001 , Vaheri et al., 2013 ). Further information is only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Proteins Hantavirids typically express three structural proteins. The most abundant structural protein in a hantavirion is N, which encapsidates the hantaviral genomic segments. The least abundant protein is L, which mediates viral genome replication and transcription. Two glycoprotein subunits, G N and G C , are produced from GPC and mediate entry of hantavirions ( Schmaljohn et al., 1985 , Spiropoulou 2001 , Vaheri et al., 2013 ). Specifics are only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Lipids Not reported but are likely derived from the Golgi apparatus and/or the host cell plasma membrane and therefore likely composed of phospholipids, glycolipids, fatty acids, and sterols. Carbohydrates Only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Genome organization and replication S RNA encodes N and in some viruses NSs ( Jääskeläinen et al., 2007 , Vera-Otarola et al., 2012 ), M RNA encodes GPC, and the L RNA encodes L with its RdRP, helicase, and endonuclease domains ( Jonsson and Schmaljohn 2001 ) (Figure 1 Hantaviridae ). Specifics are only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Figure 1 Hantaviridae . Genome organization of representative hantaviruses. The 5′- and 3′- ends of all segments are complementary at their termini, likely promoting the formation of panhandle RNP complexes within the virion . GPC , glycoprotein precursor gene; L , large (protein) gene; N , nucleoprotein gene. Biology Hantavirids have been found in actinopterygian (gobiid, lophiid, percid, ogcocephalid, and triacanthodid, and possibly goblid and melanotaeniid) and agnathan (myxinid) fish; in emballonurid, hipposiderid, pteropodid, rhinolophid, verspertillionid, and possibly molossid and nycterid bats; in soricid and talpid eulipotyphla; in muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents; in gekkonid and possibly scincid reptiles; and potentially in coleopteran and plectopteran insects (see genus pages for details). Only orthohantaviruses are known to cause diseases (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Antigenicity Systematic antigenicity studies have only been reported for orthohantaviruses (see Orthohantavirus genus page). species demarcation criteria The availability of at least coding-complete sequences of all three genome segments may be sufficient for hantavirid classification in the absence of a cultured isolate. Demarcation of genera is based upon DivErsity pArtitioning by hieRarchical Clustering (DEmARC) analysis) using concatenated deduced S, M, and L segment expression product sequences ( Hantaviridae: current classification and future perspectives, Viruses, 11, 9, e0788">Laenen et al., 2019 ). DEmARC analysis gave a frequency distribution of Pairwise Evolutionary Distance (PED) values of which the threshold of 0.1 gave an optimal clustering cost of zero and is used as the hantavirid species demarcation criterium. Genera are demarked by a PED-value threshold of 0.95 and subfamilies are demarcated based on their distinct clustering in a Bayesian maximum clade credibility tree and a PED-value threshold of 3.5. Relationships within the family Phylogenetic relationships across the family have been estimated using Bayesian maximum clade credibility trees generated from complete N, GPC, and L amino-acid sequences; similar topologies are obtained with concatenated N and GPC sequences (Figure 2 Hantaviridae ). Figure 2 Hantaviridae . Maximum likelihood phylogenetic tree inferred using IQ-TREE. The tree was constructed based on 53 concatenated S and M segment (amino acid) sequences using the LG+R9 model of sequence evolution. Branch lengths represent the estimated number of substitutions per site. Bootstrap support values (>70%) are indicated at nodes, reflecting the degree of confidence in the branching pattern. Relationships with other taxa Hantavirids are closely related to bunyaviral crulivirids, fimovirids, peribunyavirids, phasmavirids, tulasvirids, and tospovirids ( Wolf et al., 2018 , Herath et al., 2020 ). Using the Master Species List Using the Virus Metadata Resource Using the Find the Species tool Using the ICTV Report Webinar Webinar on Virus Taxonomy Webinar on Finding Information GitHub Repository Zenodo Repository Email ICTV Help ‏‏‎ ‎ ICTV Report Book: Hantaviridae Family: Hantaviridae Subfamily: Actantavirinae Genus: Actinovirus Genus: Percilovirus Subfamily: Agantavirinae Genus: Agnathovirus Subfamily: Mammantavirinae Genus: Loanvirus Genus: Mobatvirus Genus: Orthohantavirus Genus: Thottimvirus Subfamily: Repantavirinae Genus: Reptillovirus Authors: Hantaviridae Citation: Hantaviridae References: Hantaviridae Resources: Hantaviridae Species List: Hantaviridae Subfamily: Mammantavirinae Genus: Orthohantavirus Distinguishing features Sixty different viruses are classified in the genus Orthohantavius. These viruses typically infect specific soricid and talpid eulipotyphla and muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents. Orthohantaviruses are the only hantavirids known to cause disease in humans ( Schmaljohn and Hjelle 1997 , Jonsson et al., 2010 , Kuhn and Schmaljohn 2023 , Vial et al., 2023 ). Virion Morphology Orthohantavirions are pleomorphic in shape, mostly spherical of 80–160 nm in diameter ( Huiskonen et al., 2010 ), and surrounded by a membrane envelope that is decorated with glycoprotein (GP) spikes composed of G N and G C subunits (Figure 1 Orthohantavirus ). The virion envelope is 5 nm thick and is decorated with square shaped spikes, consisting of tetrameric G N -G C heterodimers, which protrude 10 nM from the membrane forming a surface lattice of local symmetry interrupted by empty membrane spots ( Hung et al., 1983 , Huiskonen et al., 2010 , Battisti et al., 2011 , Parvate et al., 2019 , Serris et al., 2020 , Guardado-Calvo and Rey 2021 ). Isolated ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes are composed of individual segment genomic RNA encapsidated by nucleoprotein (N) ( Tao et al., 1987 , Huiskonen et al., 2010 , Battisti et al., 2011 , Hepojoki et al., 2012 , Guo et al., 2016 , Arragain et al., 2019 ). Virions assemble and bud from the Golgi complex or cell surface membranes, depending on the virus ( Goldsmith et al., 1995 , Parvate et al., 2019 ). Figure 1 Orthohantavirus. A, B) Electron micrographs of Tula virus particles adapted from ( Huiskonen et al., 2010 ). C) Schematic illustration of an orthohantavirus particle. Shown is a spherical and enveloped (grey) particle with glycoprotein spikes (G N yellow, G C blue) inserted in a bilaminar lipid envelope. The S (small), M (medium), and L (large) RNP (ribonucleoprotein) complexes inside the particle consist of N (nucleoprotein, green) and L (large protein, pink). ViralZone image reproduced courtesy of SwissBioPics. Physicochemical and physical properties Virion buoyant densities in sucrose and CsCl are 1.15–1.18 ( White et al., 1982 ) and 1.20–1.21 g cm −3 , respectively ( Schmaljohn et al., 1983 ). Virions are sensitive to chemical inactivation with, for instance, methanol, paraformaldehyde, acetone/methanol, N -ethylmaleimide or detergents, as well as physical methods such as heat, gamma irradiation or UV irradiation ( Kraus et al., 2005 , Strandin et al., 2011 , Elveborg et al., 2022 ). Nucleic acid Orthohantavirus genomes are linear tri-segmented RNA molecules of negative polarity. The genomes are about 11.1–12.3 kb in length (small [S] segment: 1.2–2.1 kb; medium [M] segment: 3.4–3.8 kb; large [L] segment: 6.5–6.6 kb). Proteins Orthohantaviruses typically express three structural proteins (Table 1 Orthohantavirus ). The most abundant structural protein in an orthohantavirion is N, which encapsidates the orthohantaviral genomic segments. The least abundant protein is L, which mediates viral genome replication and transcription. Two glycoprotein subunits, G N and G C , mediate virion entry. G N and G C and non-structural proteins are encoded as a precursor polyprotein. Table 1 Orthohantavirus . Location and function of orthohantavirus structural proteins. Protein Location, mass, and function Reference Nucleoprotein (N) Structural virion protein (about 48 kD). Oligomerizes and encapsidates orthohantaviral genomic segments and hence component of RNPs. Binds to L and G N ( Mir et al., 2010 , Reuter and Krüger 2018 , Arragain et al., 2019 ) Nonstructural protein (NSs) Non-structural protein encoded by some orhtohantaviruses. Has type I interferon inhibitory activity. May occur as multiple isoforms. ( Vera-Otarola et al., 2020 , Binder et al., 2021 ) Glycoprotein (GP) Structural virion protein consisting of two subunits (G N : about 70-75 kD, G C : about 50-55 kD). Produced via proteolytic cleavage from the genome-encoded precursor GPC. Projects from virion membranes as tetrameric GP spikes composed of G N and G C heterodimers. GP mediates cell- receptor binding; as a class II fusion machine it induces virion-cell membrane fusion and, thereby cell entry. G N binds to N and RNA ( Spiropoulou et al., 2003 , Tischler et al., 2005 , Cifuentes-Muñoz et al., 2014 , Li et al., 2016 , Willensky et al., 2016 , Rissanen et al., 2017 , Zhu et al., 2018 , Bignon et al., 2019 , Sperber et al., 2019 ) Large protein (L) Structural virion protein (246 kD) with RdRP, helicase, and endoribonuclease domains. Component of the RNP inside virions. Binds to N and RNA. Oligomerizes and mediates transcription and replication of viral RNA segments. Mediates cap-snatching for viral mRNA capping. ( Kukkonen et al., 2005 , Cheng et al., 2014 , Rothenberger et al., 2016 , Jeeva et al., 2019 , Durieux Trouilleton et al., 2023 ) Genome organization and replication The orthohantavirus genome consists of three negative-sense RNA molecules, termed S (small), M (medium), and L (large) (Figure 2 Orthohantavirus ). Figure 2 Orthohantavirus. Schematic representation of orthohantavirus genome organization. Orthohantavirus genomic segments assume circular forms via non-covalent binding of complementary and highly conserved 3′- and 5′-terminal sequences. Genomic segment reassortment mostly occurs among viruses belonging to the same species but interspecies reassortment likely occurs occasionally ( Klempa 2018 , Petazzi et al., 2021 ). Orthohantavirus infection starts with virion attachment, mediated by G N and G C , to cell-surface attachment factors and entry via the endosomal route ( Shtanko et al., 2014 ) (Figure 3 Orthohantavirus ). Figure 3 Orthohantavirus . Lifecycle of orthohantaviruses. (1) Virion attachment; (2) virion uptake; (3) virion-cell membrane fusion; (4) transcription; (5) translation; (6) replication; (7) virion assembly; and (8) virion egress. After engaging a cellular receptor, protocadherin 1 in the case of American orthohantaviruses, virion-membrane fusion results in early or late endosomal release, depending on the virus, of the virion RNP complex into the cytoplasm in a pH-dependent manner ( Jangra et al., 2018 , Mittler et al., 2019 , Torriani et al., 2019 , Dieterle et al., 2021 ). During primary transcription L generates uncapped antigenomic RNA molecules that are then capped using host cell-derived capped primers (cap snatching). L and S segment-transcribed mRNAs are translated by free ribosomes ( Garcin et al., 1995 , Jeeva et al., 2019 , Meier et al., 2021 ). M segment-transcribed mRNA is translated by membrane-bound ribosomes, with the expressed GPC which is likely co-translationally cleaved by cellular proteases to yield G N and G C . The synthesis of the antigenome by L protein serves as a template for genomic RNA replication. Secondary transcription amplifies the synthesis of mRNAs and genome replication. During morphogenesis, G N and G C accumulate in the Golgi apparatus, modified host membranes are acquired, and virions bud into the Golgi. Biology Genus Orthohantavirus includes 38 species for 60 distinct viruses. These viruses and their unclassified, potential relatives, subclinically, and often chronically, infect specific soricid and talpid eulipotyphla, and muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents ( Jonsson et al., 2010 , Wu et al., 2018 , Chen et al., 2023 , Kuhn and Schmaljohn 2023 ). Orthohantaviruses are overall distributed worldwide, but the individual geographic distribution is dependent on host range. At least some orthohantaviruses may not be as restricted to a particular host as originally thought, but may be carried by animals of multiple hosts ( Goodfellow et al., 2021 , Quizon et al., 2022 , Gu et al., 2023 ). Orthohantaviruses are the only hantavirids known to cause disease (all in humans) and all disease-causing viruses are rodent-borne. Human infection may occur after inhalation of aerosolized excreta or secreta of infected rodents or direct rodent contact. The two WHO-recognized orthohantavirus-caused diseases are hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), caused by Asian and European viruses (in particular Dobrava virus [DOBV], Hantaan virus [HTNV], Puumala virus [PUUV] and Seoul virus [SEOV]), and hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), a frequently lethal disease caused by viruses from the Americas (in particular Andes virus [ANDV] and Sin Nombre virus [SNV]) ( Vial et al., 2023 ). The hamster model of wild-type ANDV infection is lethal and largely mimics human HPS ( Hooper et al., 2001 ). After SNV infection in nonhuman primates, some animals develop an HPS-like disease, but cell passage of SNV can result in mutations that render the virus non-pathogenic in this model ( Safronetz et al., 2014 ). Many rodent models result in a chronic, asymptomatic infection, and these have been used in early-stage therapeutic studies ( Strandin et al., 2020 ). However, recent advances have been made in development of an HFRS mouse model using HTNV variants ( Wei et al., 2022 ). Orthohantavirus animal models are reviewed in ( Golden et al., 2015 ). Antigenicity There is considerable serum cross-reactivity between the nucleocapsids of hantavirids, but neutralizing antibodies targeting Gn/Gc are more specific. SNV was first identified as a hantavirid based on cross-reactivity of patient sera with other orthohantavirus antigens ( 1993 ). Similarly, rodents that carried SNV were identified in serosurveys using non-SNV orthohantavirus antigens, since SNV had not been isolated at the time ( Childs et al., 1994 ). Species demarcation criteria Demarcation of species is based upon DivErsity pArtitioning by hieRarchical Clustering (DEmARC) analysis) using concatenated deduced S, M, and L segment expression product sequences ( Laenen et al., 2019 ). Phylogenetic relationships across the genus have been estimated using maximum likelihood trees generated from complete N, GPC and L amino-acid sequences, and for N and GPC amino-acid sequences (Figure 2 Hantaviridae ). GENOME Segmented Negative-stranded RNA linear genome, L segment is between 6.8 and 12 kb, M segment between 3.2 and 4.9 kb and S segment between 1 and 3 kb. Encodes for four to six proteins. Some hantaviruses also encode a NSs protein on their S segment. GENE EXPRESSION The viral RNA dependent RNA polymerase (L) binds to a promoter on each encapsidated segment, and transcribes the mRNA. These are capped by L protein during synthesis using cap snatching . Transcription is terminated by a strong hairpin sequence at the end of each gene. Puumala virus expressed an additional NSs by leaky scanning in the NS gene. ENZYMES RNA-dependent RNA polymerase L Cap Snatching endonuclease L REPLICATION CYTOPLASMIC Virus attaches to host receptors though Gn-Gc glycoprotein dimer, and is endocytosed into vesicles in the host cell. Fusion of virus membrane with the vesicle membrane; ribonucleocapsid segments are released in the cytoplasm. Transcription , viral mRNAs are capped in the cytoplasm. Replication presumably starts when enough nucleoprotein is present to encapsidate neo-synthetized antigenomes and genomes. The ribonucleocapsids buds at Golgi apparatus, releasing the virion by exocytosis. The hantaviruses (Hantaviridae) ~ ViralZone Skip to main content ViralZone Back to Andes virus resource There are approximately 92 known viruses in the family Hantaviridae, classified into 52 species. Each species is typically adapted to a specific reservoir host, most commonly rodents, but also bats and moles. With the notable exception of Andes virus, hantaviruses are generally not transmitted from person to person. Based on their geographic distribution, evolutionary relationships, and the diseases they cause in humans, hantaviruses can be broadly divided into three major groups: New World hantaviruses (the Americas) These viruses cause Hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), a severe respiratory disease. Important examples include Sin Nombre virus and Andes virus. Annual incidence are about 100 cases per year (Andes virus) about 25 cases per year (Sin Nombre virus) Old World hantaviruses (Asia) These viruses are responsible for Hantavirus hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), which is characterized by fever, hemorrhage, and acute kidney injury. Major examples include Hantaan virus and Seoul virus. Annual incidence: more than 10,000 cases worldwide Old World hantaviruses (Europe) European hantaviruses typically cause a milder form of HFRS known as Nephropathia epidemica (NE). The main causative agents are Puumala virus and Dobrava-Belgrade virus. Annual incidence: more than 1,000 cases Together, these viruses represent an important and diverse group of zoonotic pathogens that can cause severe disease following accidental transmission from their natural animal hosts to humans.

papers.title: CD8+ regulatory T cells limit immunopathology but impair viral clearance in Hantaan virus infection.
papers.abstract: In hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) caused by Hantaan virus (HTNV), virus-specific CD8 + T cells mediate both viral clearance and immunopathology. Here, we characterized a CD8 + regulatory T cell (Treg) subset restricted by HLA-E (and its murine ortholog Qa-1) in HFRS patients and in a murine HTNV infection model. CD8 + Tregs (CD122 + Eomes + CD49d lo KIR + ), a subset substantially enriched for HLA-E-restricted T cells, were significantly reduced in peripheral blood of HFRS patients and displayed a terminally differentiated profile with elevated expression of KLRG-1, NKG2A, CTLA-4, and Fas-L, correlating with disease severity. Two HTNV glycoprotein-derived nonapeptides that bound Qa-1 were identified. Following immunization with the identified HTNV peptides and subsequent HTNV challenge, wild-type (WT) mice showed attenuated renal immunopathology, whereas D227K knock-in mice (with disrupted Qa-1-CD8/TCR interaction) showed enhanced viral clearance in the spleen and kidney but exacerbated renal immunopathology. Mechanistically, Qa-1-restricted CD8 + Tregs from WT mice suppressed effector CD8 + T cell proliferation in a peptide-specific, CD8/TCR-dependent manner via enhanced TGF-β secretion. Strikingly, D227K mutation dichotomously reshaped Treg phenotype: bulk polyclonal CD8 + Tregs displayed compensatory upregulation of inhibitory receptors (NKG2A, CTLA-4, PD-1) and TGF-β, whereas epitope-specific CD8 + Tregs showed impaired antigen-specific suppressive function and attenuated TGF-β production. Collectively, these findings indicate that HLA-E/Qa-1-restricted CD8 + Tregs can restrain immunopathology during HTNV infection, potentially at the cost of delayed viral elimination. Modulation of this axis may provide insights for therapeutic strategies in HFRS and related viral hemorrhagic fevers.
papers.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America

papers.title: Molecular evolution of Andes virus lineages leading to recent human outbreaks
papers.abstract: Andes virus (ANDV) is exceptional among hantaviruses in its capacity for person-to-person transmission, but whether outbreaks reflect recent viral adaptation or emergence of pre-existing reservoir lineages remains unclear. We generated paired blood- and nasal-derived genomes from the MV Hondius outbreak and integrated them with a segment-linked collection of human- and rodent-derived ANDV sequences, including incomplete genomes. We developed a linkage-informed missing-segment framework that preserves isolate identity, sampling time, and cross-segment placement without imputing nucleotide states, enabling sensitivity analyses of patchy segment coverage. Across five human outbreaks, dated phylogenies placed outbreak lineages independently within geographically structured reservoir diversity, with closest sampled ancestry predating detection. Time-dependent-rate analyses indicated a deeper reservoir-associated history, while mutation reconstruction, selection tests, branch-rate comparisons, and structural mapping found no recurrent adaptive transition preceding human transmission. MV Hondius samples showed minimal consensus-level diversification. These results shift attention from repeated recent adaptation toward deeper lineage properties and ecological opportunity.

analysis_zh.background: 安第斯病毒(ANDV)在汉坦病毒中因人际传播而显得异常,且尚不清楚近期暴发是反映新的病毒适应还是先前存在的储备宿主谱系的出现。
analysis_zh.methods: 从MV Hondius暴发中获取的血液和鼻腔配对基因组被构建并与一套人类和啮齿动物来源的ANDV序列(包括不完整基因组)的节段关联集合整合;采用了基于关联信息的缺失节段框架,保留分离株身份、采样时间和跨节段定位。
analysis_zh.results: 经年代标定的系统发育树将暴发谱系独立定位于地理结构化的储备宿主多样性中,最近的采样祖先早于检测出现;时间依赖速率分析显示更深的储备宿主相关历史,且突变重建、选择检验、分支速率比较和结构映射均未发现在人际传播前的重复适应性转变;MV Hondius样本显示出极低的共识水平多样化。
analysis_zh.contribution: 这些结果将关注点从反复的近期适应转向更深层的谱系特性和生态机会,作为人类暴发的驱动因素。
analysis_zh.limitations: 仅有摘要信息;未在提供的证据中报告详细方法、样本量、地点和定量统计数据。

papers.title: Persistent leukopenia masks hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome.
papers.abstract: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) typically comes with fever, facial flushing, rash, thrombocytopenia, acute kidney injury, coagulopathy and leukocytosis. However, atypical manifestations may obscure diagnosis. A 30-year-old man with rodent exposure had high fever, thrombocytopenia, and persistent leukopenia, without overt renal dysfunction despite mild renal involvement in the form of proteinuria. Hantaan virus was confirmed by serology and RT-PCR. The patient recovered following ribavirin and supportive management. This case highlights that in HFRS-endemic regions, hantavirus infection should be suspected among patients with unexplained fever, thrombocytopenia, and persistent leukopenia rather than the typical leukocytosis, even without overt renal dysfunction.

analysis.background: HFRS typically presents with fever, facial flushing, rash, thrombocytopenia, acute kidney injury, coagulopathy and leukocytosis, but atypical manifestations may obscure diagnosis.
analysis.methods: A single 30‑year‑old man with rodent exposure was evaluated; clinical findings and laboratory testing (serology and RT‑PCR) confirmed Hantaan virus infection.
analysis.results: The patient had high fever, thrombocytopenia, persistent leukopenia and mild proteinuria without overt renal dysfunction; Hantaan virus was identified and he recovered after ribavirin and supportive care.
analysis.contribution: The case highlights that in HFRS‑endemic regions hantavirus infection should be suspected in patients with unexplained fever, thrombocytopenia and persistent leukopenia, even without typical leukocytosis or overt renal failure.
analysis.limitations: The report is limited to an abstract of a single case, providing no detailed methodology, broader epidemiologic context, or long‑term outcomes.

analysis.summary_en: Background: HFRS usually shows fever, rash, thrombocytopenia, AKI, coagulopathy and leukocytosis, yet atypical signs can mask it. Methods: One 30‑year‑old man with rodent exposure was assessed; serology and RT‑PCR confirmed Hantaan virus. Results: He presented with high fever, thrombocytopenia, persistent leukopenia and mild proteinuria, recovered after ribavirin. Contribution: The case alerts clinicians in endemic areas to consider hantavirus infection despite absent leukocytosis or clear renal failure. Limitations: Only an abstract of a single case is available, lacking detailed methods and broader data.

papers.title_zh: 持续性白细胞减少掩盖了肾综合征出血热。

analysis_zh.background: 肾综合征出血热通常表现为发热、面部潮红、皮疹、血小板减少、急性肾损伤、凝血功能障碍和白细胞增多,但非典型表现可能掩盖诊断。
analysis_zh.methods: 对一名有啮齿动物暴露史的30岁男性进行评估;临床表现和实验室检测(血清学和RT‐PCR)确认了 汉滩病毒 感染。
analysis_zh.results: 患者出现高热、血小板减少、持续性白细胞减少和轻度蛋白尿,但无明显肾功能障碍;鉴定为 汉滩病毒,经利巴韦林和支持治疗后恢复。
analysis_zh.contribution: 该病例提示,在肾综合征出血热流行地区,即使患者出现不明原因发热、血小板减少和持续性白细胞减少,且缺乏典型的白细胞增多或明显的肾功能衰竭,也应考虑 汉坦病毒 感染。
analysis_zh.limitations: 本报告仅为单例摘要,未提供详细方法、更广的流行病学背景或长期结局。

papers.title: Hantavirus Disease in a Changing World: Reservoir Ecology, Endothelial Dysfunction, Clinical Management, and the 2026 M/V Hondius Andes Virus Outbreak
papers.abstract: Hantaviruses are zoonotic, tri-segmented negative-sense RNA viruses maintained in diverse mammalian reservoirs. Human disease is caused predominantly by orthohantaviruses and manifests chiefly as hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) in Eurasia or hantavirus pulmonary/cardiopulmonary syndrome (HPS/HCPS) in the Americas. Andes virus (ANDV) is epidemiologically distinctive because limited human-to-human transmission has been repeatedly documented. This update-oriented narrative review synthesizes evidence available through to 28 August 2026 and is organized around an integrative framework linking reservoir ecology and spillover, ANDV-specific person-to-person transmission, endothelial and immune dysfunction, clinical phenotype, critical-care management, and One Health preparedness. The recent 2026 M/V Hondius outbreak is used as a case study of how a primarily rodent-borne infection can generate international operational consequences in a mobile, closed setting. Recent HFRS surveillance from Asia and Europe is included to balance the ANDV-focused outbreak analysis. Severe disease is associated with endothelial barrier dysfunction, capillary leak, thrombocytopenia, myocardial or renal involvement, and dysregulated host responses rather than widespread endothelial necrosis. Current evidence supports early recognition and organ support; evidence for ribavirin, immune plasma, monoclonal antibodies, and host-directed vascular therapies differs substantially by syndrome and remains limited or investigational for HPS/HCPS. The M/V Hondius event ultimately involved 13 cases (12 confirmed and one probable) and three deaths, with no further secondary cases after completion of international follow-up.

analysis.background: The review updates hantavirus knowledge through 28 August 2026, motivated by the need to integrate reservoir ecology, spillover, and clinical management in a changing world.
analysis.main_directions: It covers reservoir ecology, ANDV‑specific person‑to‑person transmission, endothelial and immune dysfunction, clinical phenotypes, critical‑care strategies, and One Health preparedness, illustrated by the 2026 M/V Hondius outbreak.
analysis.current_state: Severe hantavirus disease is linked to endothelial barrier dysfunction and capillary leak rather than necrosis, and early recognition with organ support improves outcomes.
analysis.gaps: Therapeutic evidence (ribavirin, immune plasma, monoclonal antibodies, vascular‑targeted agents) remains limited or investigational, especially for HPS/HCPS, and data on sustained human‑to‑human spread are sparse.
analysis.future_research: Rigorous clinical trials of antivirals and host‑directed therapies, plus longitudinal surveillance of ANDV transmission dynamics and One Health response capacity, are needed.

analysis.summary_en: Background: The review updates hantavirus knowledge to 28 Aug 2026, linking ecology and clinical care. Main directions: It integrates reservoir ecology, ANDV person‑to‑person spread, endothelial dysfunction, clinical phenotypes, critical‑care management, and One Health preparedness, using the M/V Hondius outbreak as a case study. Current state: Severe disease stems from endothelial barrier failure and early organ‑support improves outcomes. Gaps: Therapeutic evidence is limited, especially for HPS/HCPS, and human‑to‑human transmission data are incomplete. Future research: Conduct robust trials of antivirals and vascular therapies and enhance surveillance of ANDV transmission and preparedness.

analysis_zh.background: 本综述更新了截至2026年8月28日的汉坦病毒知识,动因是需要在不断变化的世界中整合宿主生态、跨种传播以及临床管理。
analysis_zh.main_directions: 内容涵盖宿主生态、安第斯病毒特异性的人际传播、内皮与免疫功能失调、临床表型、重症监护策略以及 One Health 应急准备,并以2026年 M/V Hondius 事件为例。
analysis_zh.current_state: 严重的汉坦病毒疾病与内皮屏障功能障碍和毛细血管渗漏有关,而非坏死;早期识别并给予器官支持可改善预后。
analysis_zh.gaps: 治疗证据(利巴韦林、免疫血浆、单克隆抗体、血管靶向制剂)仍然有限或处于研究阶段,尤其针对 HPS/HCPS;关于持续的人际传播的数据亦十分稀缺。
analysis_zh.future_research: 需要开展严格的抗病毒药物和宿主靶向疗法临床试验,并进行安第斯病毒传播动态的长期监测以及 One Health 应对能力的评估。

papers.title: Hantavirus infection and the boundaries of autoimmunity: Vascular immunopathology, autoimmune-like mimicry, and post-infectious phenomena.
papers.abstract: Orthohantaviruses are rodent-borne RNA viruses causing acute systemic vascular syndromes, principally haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome. Although primarily infectious, hantavirus disease may generate vascular, renal, haematological, and systemic phenotypes that overlap with immune-mediated disorders. This Review critically examines the boundary between infection-driven immunopathology and autoimmunity. Hantavirus infection involves endothelial dysfunction, innate antiviral sensing, interferon responses, cytokine and chemokine amplification, complement activation, immunothrombosis, and adaptive immune responses, whose expression is further influenced by virus-, host-, and tissue-specific factors. These mechanisms contribute to the marked heterogeneity of clinical disease and may reproduce autoimmune-like clinical and laboratory features, but do not, in themselves, establish sustained loss of immune tolerance. Current evidence is substantially stronger for acute infection-associated immunopathology and phenotypic mimicry than for persistent autoreactivity or causally attributable post-infectious autoimmune disease. Reported autoimmune phenomena remain uncommon and predominantly case-based, while longitudinal, antigen-specific, and epidemiological evidence is limited. Persistent or recurrent manifestations after resolution of infection therefore require additional serological, histopathological, or other objective evidence of sustained immune dysregulation. Hantavirus infection thus provides a clinically informative model for distinguishing antiviral immunopathology from autoimmune-like mimicry and rare possible post-infectious autoimmunity, with direct implications for diagnosis and therapeutic restraint. TAKE-HOME MESSAGES.

papers.title_zh: 汉坦病毒感染与自身免疫边界:血管免疫病理、自身免疫样模仿及感染后现象。

analysis_zh.background: 正汉坦病毒是啮齿动物传播的RNA病毒,导致急性全身血管综合征,如肾综合征出血热和汉坦病毒心肺综合征。
analysis_zh.main_directions: 综述指出,汉坦病毒疾病可产生血管、肾脏、血液学及全身表型,与免疫介导的疾病重叠,其机制包括内皮功能障碍、先天感知、干扰素、细胞因子/趋化因子放大、补体活化、免疫血栓形成以及适应性免疫。
analysis_zh.current_state: 现有证据强有力地支持急性感染驱动的免疫病理和类自身免疫的模拟,而持续的免疫耐受丧失或感染后自身免疫疾病的证据则较为薄弱。
analysis_zh.gaps: 已报道的自身免疫现象罕见,主要基于病例,缺乏纵向、抗原特异性和流行病学的确认。
analysis_zh.future_research: 需要进一步的血清学、组织病理学和纵向研究,以证明在汉坦病毒痊愈后持续的免疫失调。

papers.title: A single-amino acid difference between rodent and human Andes virus affects viral glycoprotein trafficking.
papers.abstract: Andes virus (ANDV) causes hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), with rare outbreaks involving person-to-person transmission. A human ANDV isolate from one such outbreak and a rodent isolate from the same region differ in lethality in Syrian golden hamsters. Genomic analysis revealed 25 nonsynonymous substitutions, including one leading to a T641I change in the human ANDV glycoprotein precursor near its cleavage site. Although the isolates differed in growth kinetics, strand-specific RT-qPCR did not support major differences in viral RNA synthesis, whereas virion release was delayed in the case of the human isolate. In human cell expression systems, a single I641T substitution in the human ANDV glycoprotein resulted in decreased Golgi retention and faster release of virion-like particles relative to wild-type glycoprotein. Since ANDV egress takes place at the Golgi, the T641I change present in the human ANDV isolate may represent a human adaptive mutation influencing glycoprotein trafficking and virus particle release.

analysis.background: Andes virus (ANDV) causes hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), with rare outbreaks involving person-to-person transmission.
analysis.methods: A human ANDV isolate from an outbreak and a rodent isolate from the same region were compared, including lethality testing in Syrian golden hamsters; genomic sequencing identified 25 nonsynonymous substitutions, notably a T641I change in the glycoprotein precursor; a human cell expression system was used to assess the effect of an I641T substitution on glycoprotein trafficking.
analysis.results: The human isolate showed reduced lethality in hamsters and delayed virion release despite similar viral RNA synthesis; the I641T substitution decreased Golgi retention and accelerated release of virion‑like particles relative to wild‑type glycoprotein.
analysis.contribution: The T641I change present in the human isolate may represent a human‑adaptive mutation that influences glycoprotein trafficking and virus particle release, advancing understanding of ANDV host adaptation.
analysis.limitations: Only the abstract is available; detailed experimental design, sample sizes, statistical analyses, and broader epidemiological context are not reported in the supplied evidence.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Andes virus causes HPS and can spread person‑to‑person. Methods: Human and rodent isolates were compared in hamster lethality assays, sequenced (revealing a T641I glycoprotein change), and expressed in human cells to test I641T effects. Results: The human isolate was less lethal and released virions more slowly, while I641T reduced Golgi retention and sped VLP release. Contribution: The T641I mutation may be a human‑adaptive change affecting glycoprotein trafficking and virus release. Limitations: Only abstract data are provided; experimental details and statistical information are not reported.

papers.title_zh: 啮齿动物与人类之间的单个氨基酸差异 安第斯病毒 影响病毒糖蛋白的运输。

analysis_zh.background: 安第斯病毒(ANDV)导致汉坦病毒肺综合征(HPS),偶尔出现人际传播的罕见爆发。
analysis_zh.methods: 对来自一次爆发的人类安第斯病毒分离株与同一地区的啮齿动物分离株进行比较,包括在叙利亚金仓鼠中进行致死性测试;基因组测序发现25个非同义突变,尤其是糖蛋白前体中的T641I变化;使用人细胞表达系统评估I641T突变对糖蛋白运输的影响。
analysis_zh.results: 人类分离株在仓鼠中的致死性降低,且在病毒RNA合成相似的情况下,病毒颗粒释放延迟;I641T突变降低了高尔基体滞留,促进了相较于野生型糖蛋白的病毒样颗粒释放。
analysis_zh.contribution: 人类分离株中的T641I变化可能代表一种人类适应性突变,影响糖蛋白运输和病毒颗粒释放,推动对安第斯病毒宿主适应性的认识。
analysis_zh.limitations: 仅提供摘要;未报告详细实验设计、样本量、统计分析及更广泛的流行病学背景。

papers.title: Hantavirus Outbreak Caused by Andes Virus Linked to International Cruise Ship Travel - United States, 2026.
papers.abstract: Andes virus (ANDV), the only hantavirus known to be transmitted person-to-person, is endemic to areas of South America and can cause hantavirus pulmonary syndrome, which has a case-fatality rate of approximately 40%. On May 4, 2026, CDC was notified of seven cases of severe acute respiratory illness, including three deaths, among 147 persons aboard a cruise ship in the Atlantic Ocean; the illnesses were later confirmed to be caused by ANDV. No cases occurred among passengers who were U.S. residents. Ten of 28 U.S. resident passengers disembarked before ANDV infection was confirmed aboard the ship. On May 10, the remaining 18 U.S. resident passengers were repatriated to the National Quarantine Unit in Omaha, Nebraska, for risk assessment and monitoring, and where optimized advanced care was available, should symptoms develop. CDC and U.S. health departments monitored 60 additional U.S. residents potentially exposed on flights involving a passenger with symptomatic ANDV infection from the cruise, totaling 88 contacts across 27 jurisdictions. All 88 contacts completed 42 days of monitoring, with no secondary ANDV infections identified. Worldwide, local health authorities assessed and monitored approximately 653 potentially exposed persons from 33 countries. This response highlights the value of rapid coordination among partners to locate and monitor potentially exposed persons during an international outbreak to reduce the risk for ANDV transmission. Prompt notification to public health authorities can facilitate testing, patient care, contact identification, and implementation of measures to limit secondary transmission.
papers.journal: MMWR. Morbidity and mortality weekly report

analysis.background: Andes virus (ANDV) is the only hantavirus known to be transmitted person‑to‑person, is endemic to South America, and can cause hantavirus pulmonary syndrome with an approximate 40% case‑fatality rate.
analysis.methods: CDC was notified on 4 May 2026 of seven severe acute respiratory illness cases (including three deaths) among 147 cruise‑ship passengers; laboratory testing confirmed ANDV infection, and contact tracing with monitoring was instituted for exposed individuals.
analysis.results: No cases occurred among U.S. passengers; 88 U.S. contacts across 27 jurisdictions completed 42‑day monitoring with no secondary ANDV infections identified; worldwide, health authorities assessed approximately 653 potentially exposed persons from 33 countries.
analysis.contribution: The response highlights the value of rapid coordination among partners to locate and monitor potentially exposed persons, facilitating testing, patient care, contact identification, and measures to limit secondary transmission during an international outbreak.
analysis.limitations: Only the abstract is available, so detailed epidemiologic methods, source investigation, and full data are not reported.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Andes virus (ANDV) is the only hantavirus known to transmit person‑to‑person and causes hantavirus pulmonary syndrome with ~40% case‑fatality. Methods: CDC identified seven severe respiratory cases (three deaths) among 147 cruise‑ship passengers on 4 May 2026; infections were laboratory‑confirmed as ANDV and contacts were traced and monitored. Results: No cases occurred among U.S. passengers; 88 U.S. contacts across 27 jurisdictions completed 42‑day monitoring with no secondary infections; worldwide 653 potential exposures from 33 countries were assessed. Contribution: The investigation demonstrates the importance of rapid inter‑agency coordination, contact identification, and monitoring to limit secondary ANDV transmission during an international outbreak. Limitations: Only the abstract is available, so detailed epidemiologic methods, source investigation, and full data are not reported.

papers.title: Progress in antiviral and vaccine strategies against hantavirus: Current advances and future perspectives
papers.abstract: Hantaviruses are rodent-associated zoonotic RNA viruses responsible for hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS), two clinically distinct diseases characterized by vascular dysfunction and potentially severe organ failure. Their geographic distribution, antigenic diversity, and variable clinical outcomes complicate the development of broadly applicable medical countermeasures. The aim of this narrative review is to critically examine the molecular rationale, current evidence, and translational readiness of antiviral and vaccine strategies against hantavirus infections. Antiviral approaches include ribavirin, favipiravir, RNA interference, neutralizing monoclonal antibodies, and investigational host-directed therapies, with particular attention to differences between human clinical evidence and findings from cell culture or animal models. Vaccine strategies are evaluated across regionally implemented inactivated vaccines, DNA candidates assessed in early-phase human trials, and recombinant protein, viral vector, and messenger RNA platforms that remain predominantly preclinical. The review also distinguishes vaccine immunogenicity, experimental protection, durability of immune responses, and clinical effectiveness. Major barriers to translation include virus-specific therapeutic responses, narrow treatment windows, targeted delivery, antigenic diversity, and the absence of validated correlates of protective immunity. This review highlights the experimental and clinical evidence needed to advance promising antiviral and vaccine candidates toward effective strategies for prevention and treatment of hantavirus infections.

Narra Review 2026; 2 (3): e43 - http://doi.org/10.52225/narrarev.v2i3.43 Page 2 of 23 Narrative Review Introduction Hantaviruses are enveloped, tripartite, negative-sense RNA viruses within the family Hantaviridae. The genome comprises small (S), medium (M), and large (L) segments that encode proteins required for viral replication and host-cell entry [1]. Rodents are the principal reservoirs of human-pathogenic hantaviruses, and their distribution and transmission are shaped by reservoir ecology and environmental conditions [2]. Ecological analyses based largely on Chinese surveillance further emphasize that environmental variability and host population dynamics can influence hantavirus transmission [3]. Human infection is associated primarily with two major clinical syndromes: hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), most commonly reported in Asia and Europe, and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS), predominantly reported in the Americas [4,5]. HFRS is characterized by fever, vascular instability, hemorrhagic manifestations, and varying degrees of acute kidney injury [4]. In contrast, HCPS may progress rapidly to noncardiogenic pulmonary edema, respiratory failure, and circulatory shock [5]. These geographic patterns are associated with differences in circulating viral species and their reservoir hosts. Moreover, changes in land use, land cover, and human–rodent interactions may further modify exposure risks [6-8]. Human infection usually follows inhalation of aerosols contaminated with urine, feces, or saliva from infected rodents, particularly during activities that disturb contaminated materials [9]. Epidemiological investigations have identified residential, occupational, and recreational exposures among patients with HCPS in the United States [10]. Human-to-human transmission is uncommon but has been documented for Andes virus, typically in circumstances involving close or prolonged contact [9,11]. Accordingly, current prevention strategies primarily focus on reducing human exposure to infected rodents and their excreta, particularly in potentially contaminated residential and occupational environments [12]. Vascular endothelial cells are major targets of pathogenic hantaviruses, and clinically significant vascular leakage can develop without extensive direct virus-mediated cytolysis [13]. Altered vascular endothelial growth factor signaling has been implicated in endothelial barrier integrity in experimental systems [14]. Innate and adaptive immune responses contribute to viral control but may also exacerbate inflammation and vascular dysfunction, suggesting that therapeutic strategies may need to address both viral replication and dysregulated host responses [15,16]. Recent surveillance data illustrate the continuing, geographically heterogeneous disease burden. In China, national surveillance recorded 3,271 cases of epidemic hemorrhagic fever and 16 deaths in 2025 [17]. In the European Union/European Economic Area (EU/EEA), 1,885 hantavirus infections were reported in 2023, corresponding to a notification rate of 0.4 cases per 100,000 population [18]. In the Americas, the Pan American Health Organization reported 229 confirmed cases of hantavirus pulmonary syndrome and 59 deaths through epidemiological week 47 of 2025, corresponding to a reported case-fatality proportion of 25.7% [19]. These figures originate from different years, surveillance systems, and case definitions and should not be interpreted as directly comparable estimates of regional incidence or disease lethality. Despite this burden, supportive management remains the cornerstone of clinical care, and no antiviral has demonstrated consistent efficacy across HFRS and HCPS [9]. A randomized clinical trial conducted in China reported reduced mortality and selected complications among patients with HFRS receiving intravenous ribavirin [20]. However, a placebo-controlled trial in HCPS did not establish a clinical benefit during the cardiopulmonary phase, underscoring why treatment findings cannot be generalized across syndromes or disease stages [21]. Favipiravir has shown antiviral activity and improved survival under selected preclinical conditions [22]. RNA interference has suppressed Andes virus replication in cultured cells [23]. Neutralizing monoclonal antibodies have conferred protection in selected animal challenge models, but their efficacy in patients remains unconfirmed [24]. Collectively, these findings illustrate the different levels of evidence supporting current antiviral candidates, ranging from clinical investigation to in vitro and animal-model studies [25]. Prevention faces similar translational challenges. Inactivated vaccines targeting HFRS- associated hantaviruses have been implemented in China [26], while Hantavax is an authorized Khairullah et al. Narra Review 2026; 2 (3): e43 - http://doi.org/10.52225/narrarev.v2i3.43 Page 3 of 23 Narrative Review inactivated Hantaan virus vaccine in South Korea [27]. In contrast, a bivalent Hantaan/Puumala DNA vaccine has reached phase IIa clinical evaluation for safety and immunogenicity, without demonstrating clinical effectiveness against naturally acquired infection [28]. Recombinant protein, viral vector-based, and messenger RNA vaccine platforms have been investigated predominantly in preclinical studies, and the breadth and durability of vaccine-induced protection remain important evidence gaps [29]. Accordingly, the aim of this narrative review is to critically evaluate the molecular rationale, evidence levels, and translational limitations of current hantavirus antiviral and vaccine strategies. The discussion first summarizes mechanisms relevant to therapeutic targeting and antigen design, then compares clinically investigated interventions with preclinical and exploratory approaches, assesses the development status of vaccine platforms, and identifies priorities for further experimental and clinical validation. Virology and pathogenesis of hantavirus Genome organization and viral structure The hantavirus genome comprises three RNA segments, each encoding proteins with distinct roles in the viral life cycle. The S segment encodes the nucleocapsid (N) protein, which encapsidates viral RNA and participates in viral RNA synthesis [1]. The M segment encodes a glycoprotein precursor processed into the surface glycoproteins Gn and Gc, which mediate viral attachment and membrane fusion [30]. Because Gn and Gc contain neutralizing antibody epitopes, they represent important targets for antibody-based interventions and vaccine antigen design [31−33]. Furthermore, the ability of Gn and Gc to self-assemble into virus-like particles in experimental expression systems provides a potential platform for vaccine antigen presentation [34]. The L segment encodes the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp), which is responsible for viral messenger RNA (mRNA) transcription and genome replication [1]. During transcription, the viral transcription machinery uses short capped RNA primers acquired from host transcripts through cap-snatching to synthesize mRNA from negative-sense genomic RNA (vRNA) [35]. In contrast, genome replication proceeds through primer-independent synthesis of a full-length positive-sense complementary RNA (cRNA), or antigenome, from the vRNA template [36]. The antigenome subsequently serves as an intermediate template for producing new negative-sense genomic RNA, rather than functioning as a protein-coding transcript [37]. These mechanistically distinct steps identify RdRp and viral RNA synthesis as relevant targets for direct-acting antivirals. In addition, experimental evidence demonstrating interactions between N and RdRp highlights the importance of the viral replication complex in RNA synthesis [38]. Viral entry and host interaction Hantavirus entry begins with Gn/Gc-mediated interactions with host-cell entry factors, followed by endocytosis and membrane fusion within endosomal compartments [13,30]. Earlier cell-based studies implicated αvβ3 integrins in entry by certain HFRS-associated hantaviruses [39]. In contrast, protocadherin-1 (PCDH1) has been experimentally identified as a critical entry factor for Andes virus and Sin Nombre virus in pulmonary endothelial cells. Disruption of PCDH1 expression also conferred protection against Andes virus challenge in hamsters [40]. These findings indicate that entry-factor dependence differs among hantaviruses and should not be represented as a single universal receptor pathway. For Hantaan virus, clathrin-dependent receptor-mediated endocytosis was demonstrated in a cell-based investigation, although this pathway should not be assumed to operate identically in all hantaviruses [41]. Gn and Gc contribute complementary functions to viral attachment, membrane fusion, and virion assembly [42]. Following entry, pathogenic hantaviruses primarily target vascular endothelial cells, where infection can impair barrier function without extensive direct viral cytolysis [13]. Experimental studies have linked enhanced vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) signaling to increased endothelial permeability [14]. Specifically, Andes virus infection of human lung endothelial cells has been associated with increased VEGF production and reduced junctional VE-cadherin, Khairullah et al. Narra Review 2026; 2 (3): e43 - http://doi.org/10.52225/narrarev.v2i3.43 Page 4 of 23 Narrative Review contributing to endothelial barrier disruption [43]. The resulting vascular leakage contributes to renal involvement in HFRS and pulmonary and cardiovascular complications in HCPS [4, 5, 44]. Furthermore, pathogenic hantaviruses have been shown to promote platelet adherence to infected endothelial cells in experimental systems, suggesting an additional mechanism contributing to vascular dysfunction [45]. The connections between viral entry, endothelial dysfunction, and organ involvement are summarized in Figure 1. Figure 1. Hantavirus structure, entry, and endothelial pathogenesis. Immunopathogenesis Host immune responses contribute to both control of hantavirus infection and the development of vascular injury. Innate recognition involving retinoic acid-inducible gene I (RIG-I)-like receptors activates type I interferon signaling and restricts Hantaan virus replication in experimental systems [46]. However, hantaviruses can modulate these antiviral pathways, and the outcome reflects interactions between viral replication and host immune regulation [37]. In a Hantaan virus model, viral interference with TRIM25-associated RIG-I-like receptor signaling was reported as a mechanism of innate immune antagonism [47]. Clinical observations in patients with Puumala virus infection further demonstrate the involvement of both innate and adaptive immune responses during hantavirus infection [48]. In addition, neutralizing antibodies targeting the Gn/Gc glycoproteins can inhibit viral entry and represent important components of vaccine development and passive immunotherapy, although their protective breadth varies depending on the antibody and viral species [24,31]. Adaptive immune responses, particularly virus-specific T-cell responses, may contribute to viral control but can also participate in immunopathology. In an endothelial-cell culture model, hantavirus-specific cytotoxic T lymphocytes increased permeability of infected endothelial monolayers, suggesting a potential mechanism of immune-mediated endothelial injury [49]. However, the extent to which this experimental mechanism contributes to vascular pathology in patients remains incompletely established. Dysregulated inflammatory mediators and VEGF- associated signaling may further impair endothelial junctions and amplify vascular leakage [14,15, 50]. These findings highlight the need to distinguish protective antiviral immunity from potentially harmful immune-mediated responses and support the investigation of Khairullah et al. Narra Review 2026; 2 (3): e43 - http://doi.org/10.52225/narrarev.v2i3.43 Page 5 of 23 Narrative Review complementary therapeutic strategies that suppress viral replication while preserving protective immunity and endothelial integrity. Current antiviral strategies against hantavirus Current management of hantavirus infection relies primarily on supportive and organ-directed care, including respiratory and hemodynamic support and renal replacement therapy when clinically indicated [9]. Although several antiviral candidates have been investigated, their levels of supporting evidence and clinical development vary substantially. Ribavirin has undergone human clinical testing, with different outcomes reported between HFRS and HCPS [20,21]. In contrast, favipiravir [22], RNA interference-based approaches [23], and neutralizing monoclonal antibodies [24] remain supported predominantly by preclinical evidence from cell-based and animal studies. Additional compounds identified through cell-based screening have demonstrated potential to interfere with hantavirus entry, although their therapeutic relevance remains to be established [51]. 7Research Center for Preclinical and Clinical Medicine, National Research and Innovation Agency (BRIN), Bogor, Indonesia; 8Applied Master's Program in Food Security, Lampung State Polytechnic, Bandar Lampung, Indonesia; 9Department of Microbiology and Parasitology, Faculty of Medicine and Health Sciences, Universitas Jambi, Jambi, Indonesia; 10Faculty of Medicine, Universitas Wijaya Kusuma Surabaya, Surabaya, Indonesia; 11Faculty of Medicine, Universitas Pembangunan Nasional Veteran Jawa Timur, Surabaya, Indonesia; 12Medical Biotechnology Research Group, Virtual Research Center for Bioinformatics and Biotechnology, Surabaya, Indonesia; 13Uttaranchal Institute of Pharmaceutical Sciences, Uttaranchal University, Dehradun, India; 14Department of Veterinary Medicine and Biotechnology, Osh State University, Osh, Kyrgyz Republic; 15Faculty of Biotechnology and Food Engineering, Ural State Agrarian University, Yekaterinburg, Russia; 16Department of Pharmaceutics, Amity Institute of Pharmacy, Amity University Uttar Pradesh, Noida, India; 17Postgraduate School, Universitas Airlangga, Surabaya, Indonesia; 18Faculty of Health Sciences, Universitas Ma Chung, Malang, Indonesia *Corresponding authors: ansori.anm@gmail.com (ANMA) and ro.llando@machung.ac.id (RR) Abstract Hantaviruses are rodent-associated zoonotic RNA viruses responsible for hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS), two clinically distinct diseases characterized by vascular dysfunction and potentially severe organ failure. Their geographic distribution, antigenic diversity, and variable clinical outcomes complicate the development of broadly applicable medical countermeasures. The aim of this narrative review is to critically examine the molecular rationale, current evidence, and translational readiness of antiviral and vaccine strategies against hantavirus infections. Antiviral approaches include ribavirin, favipiravir, RNA interference, neutralizing monoclonal antibodies, and investigational host-directed therapies, with particular attention to differences between human clinical evidence and findings from cell culture or animal models. Vaccine strategies are evaluated across regionally implemented inactivated vaccines, live-attenuated vaccines, DNA candidates assessed in early-phase human trials, recombinant protein, viral vector, and messenger RNA platforms that remain predominantly preclinical. The review also distinguishes vaccine immunogenicity, experimental protection, durability of immune responses, and clinical effectiveness. Major barriers to translation include virus-specific therapeutic responses, narrow treatment windows, targeted delivery, antigenic diversity, and the absence of validated correlates of protective immunity. This review highlights the experimental and clinical evidence needed to advance promising antiviral and vaccine candidates toward effective strategies for prevention and treatment of hantavirus infections. The genome comprises small (S), medium (M), and large (L) segments that encode proteins required for viral replication and host-cell entry [1]. Rodents are the principal reservoirs of human-pathogenic hantaviruses, and their distribution and transmission are shaped by reservoir ecology and environmental conditions [2]. Ecological analyses based largely on Chinese surveillance further emphasize that environmental variability and host population dynamics can influence hantavirus transmission [3]. Human infection is associated primarily with two major clinical syndromes: hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), most commonly reported in Asia and Europe, and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS), predominantly reported in the Americas [4,5]. HFRS is characterized by fever, vascular instability, hemorrhagic manifestations, and varying degrees of acute kidney injury [4]. In contrast, HCPS may progress rapidly to noncardiogenic pulmonary edema, respiratory failure, and circulatory shock [5]. These geographic patterns are associated with differences in circulating viral species and their reservoir hosts. Moreover, changes in land use, land cover, and human–rodent interactions may further modify exposure risks [6-8]. Human infection usually follows inhalation of aerosols contaminated with urine, feces, or saliva from infected rodents, particularly during activities that disturb contaminated materials [9]. Epidemiological investigations have identified residential, occupational, and recreational exposures among patients with HCPS in the United States [10]. Human-to-human transmission is uncommon but has been documented for Andes virus, typically in circumstances involving close or prolonged contact [9,11]. Accordingly, current prevention strategies primarily focus on reducing human exposure to infected rodents and their excreta, particularly in potentially contaminated residential and occupational environments [12]. Vascular endothelial cells are major targets of pathogenic hantaviruses, and clinically significant vascular leakage can develop without extensive direct virus-mediated cytolysis [13]. Altered vascular endothelial growth factor signaling has been implicated in endothelial barrier integrity in experimental systems [14]. Innate and adaptive immune responses contribute to viral control but may also exacerbate inflammation and vascular dysfunction, suggesting that therapeutic strategies may need to address both viral replication and dysregulated host responses [15,16]. Recent surveillance data illustrate the continuing, geographically heterogeneous disease burden. In China, national surveillance recorded 3,271 cases of epidemic hemorrhagic fever and 16 deaths in 2025 [17]. In the European Union/European Economic Area (EU/EEA), 1,885 hantavirus infections were reported in 2023, corresponding to a notification rate of 0.4 cases per 100,000 population [18]. In the Americas, the Pan American Health Organization reported 229 confirmed cases of hantavirus pulmonary syndrome and 59 deaths through epidemiological week 47 of 2025, corresponding to a reported case-fatality proportion of 25.7% [19]. papers.title: Transcriptomic Profiling of Human Type II Alveolar Epithelial Cells Following Hantaan Virus Infection
papers.abstract: This study investigated the transcriptional responses of early-passage human type II alveolar epithelial cells (AEC II) following Hantaan virus (HTNV) exposure. RNA sequencing was performed on HTNV-exposed and mock-treated AEC II at 48 hours, with three independent biological replicates per group. The analysis focused on host transcriptional responses, particularly innate immunity, interferon-related signaling, and inflammatory pathways. Study design: Six Homo sapiens samples derived from in vitro cultured human type II alveolar epithelial cells, comprising three independent biological replicates in the HTNV-exposed group and three in the mock-treated control group. Samples were collected at 48 hours after exposure or corresponding mock treatment. Sample collection year: 2022; setting: laboratory. Library strategy: RNA-Seq. Library source: TRANSCRIPTOMIC. Sequencing service provider: Shanghai NovelBio Bio-Pharm Technology, Shanghai, China. Sequencing metadata documented in the supplied method file: Illumina NovaSeq 6000; 150 bp paired-end reads; poly(A) enrichment; TruSeq Stranded mRNA Library Prep Kit. Human reference annotation: GRCh38.p13, as labeled in the expression workbooks. Dataset contents: Processed RNA-seq results, including gene counts, FPKM and TPM expression matrices, quality-control summaries, mapping statistics, differential-expression results, GO and pathway analysis results, plots and original documentation. The six sample identifiers are HTNV-1, HTNV-2, HTNV-3, MOCK-1, MOCK-2 and MOCK-3. No raw FASTQ/FQ, BAM/CRAM or SRA files are included in the supplied archive. The original results archive is preserved without internal modification; English sample metadata and an English README accompany it. Contact: Kaixuan Zhang, Department of Clinical Laboratory, General Hospital of Wanbei Coal and Electricity Group, Yongqiao District, Suzhou, Anhui 235000, China. Email: 2461539536@qq.com.

papers.title: Diagnostic accuracy of serological, molecular and rapid tests for human hantavirus disease: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Human hantavirus disease is potentially lethal and overlaps clinically with other febrile, renal, and cardiopulmonary syndromes. Diagnostic performance varies by viral species, specimen type, sampling timing, and reference standard. OBJECTIVE: To synthesize and compare the diagnostic accuracy of serologic, molecular, rapid, multiplex, and antigen-detection tests for human hantavirus infection or disease. METHODS: We conducted a systematic review and diagnostic test accuracy meta-analysis registered in PROSPERO (CRD420261398030). MEDLINE/PubMed, Embase, Scopus, and Web of Science were searched through May 20, 2026. Human studies with an eligible index test and verifiable reference standard were included. Diagnostic accuracy data were extracted when possible. Risk of bias was assessed with QUADAS-2 and certainty with GRADE-DTA. Primary meta-analyses used platform-specific univariate logit-scale models; hierarchical bivariate/HSROC sensitivity analyses were performed for eligible strata. RESULTS: Sixty-three studies were included; 24 contributed 2 × 2 data and 22 primary comparisons entered the main synthesis. ELISA/EIA showed sensitivity of 98.0% and specificity of 98.8%, with low certainty. Rapid-format assays showed sensitivity of 97.4% and specificity of 97.2%, also with low certainty. Molecular tests had specificity of 99.5% and sensitivity of 85.6%. Bivariate sensitivity analyses for ELISA/EIA and rapid-format assays produced similar estimates to the primary models. CONCLUSIONS: In the available low-certainty evidence, ELISA/EIA serology is the best-supported platform, but this is not a universal recommendation. Molecular and rapid tests may be useful in specific contexts and require prospective validation.

analysis.background: Human hantavirus disease is potentially lethal and clinically overlaps with other febrile, renal, and cardiopulmonary syndromes.
analysis.main_directions: Diagnostic performance varies by hantavirus species, specimen type, sampling timing, and reference standard, leading to comparison of serologic, molecular, rapid, multiplex, and antigen‑detection platforms.
analysis.current_state: ELISA/EIA shows ~98 % sensitivity and specificity, rapid assays ~97 % for both, and molecular tests ~86 % sensitivity and 99.5 % specificity, but certainty is low.
analysis.gaps: Evidence certainty is low and findings cannot be universally applied; prospective validation is lacking.
analysis.future_research: Prospective, well‑designed studies validating molecular and rapid tests in diverse clinical contexts are needed.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Human hantavirus disease is potentially lethal and clinically overlaps with other febrile, renal, and cardiopulmonary syndromes (A1). Main directions: Diagnostic performance varies by hantavirus species, specimen type, sampling timing, and reference standard, prompting comparison of serologic, molecular, rapid, multiplex, and antigen‑detection platforms (A2). Current state: ELISA/EIA shows ~98 % sensitivity and specificity, rapid assays ~97 % for both, and molecular tests ~86 % sensitivity and 99.5 % specificity, though certainty is low (A13‑A15). Gaps: Evidence certainty is low and findings cannot be universally applied; prospective validation is lacking (A17). Future research: Prospective, well‑designed studies validating molecular and rapid tests in diverse clinical contexts are needed (A18).

papers.title: Hantavirus: biology, immune responses, and pathogenesis.
papers.abstract: The recent Andes virus (ANDV) outbreak on the MV Hondius cruise has raised global public health alarms due to its dangerous ability to person-to-person spread. Hantavirus infections primarily manifest as hemorrhagic fever with Eurasian renal syndrome (HFRS) and Americas hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS), both characterized by endothelial manifestation. Two principal mechanisms, virus-mediated cytopathy and host-driven immunopathology, have been proposed to account for the pathological progression, while their interplay is yet to be fully explored. In this review, we synthesize the recent research on hantavirus biology, cellular entry mechanisms, and epidemiological characteristics, and particularly highlight that viral immune evasion and subsequent uncontrolled host immune responses act as the core pathogenic drivers. Hantaviruses employ diverse strategies to antagonize type I interferon signaling and autophagy, which delay early innate immune activation and enable extensive viral dissemination. The excessive activation of cytotoxic CD8+ T cells, natural killer (NK) cells, combined with functionally impaired regulatory T cells and dysregulated humoral immunity, initiates severe inflammatory cascades, which in turn disrupt endothelial barrier integrity and cause organ vasculopathy. We also outline current therapeutic and preventive strategies, along with key directions for future research. A better understanding of hantavirus immunopathogenesis will help develop improved countermeasures against this zoonotic disease.

analysis_zh.background: 近期在邮轮上的安第斯病毒疫情引发全球公共卫生关注,促使对汉坦病毒的生物学和疾病进行综述。
analysis_zh.main_directions: 本综述概述了两大临床综合征(HFRS 与 HCPS),并强调病毒进入、免疫逃逸以及宿主免疫失调为核心主题。
analysis_zh.current_state: 目前的认识指出病毒介导的细胞病变和宿主驱动的免疫病理是主要致病机制,汉坦病毒蛋白拮抗I型干扰素和自噬。
analysis_zh.gaps: 病毒免疫逃逸策略与随之而来的失控宿主免疫反应之间的确切相互作用仍缺乏明确阐明。
analysis_zh.future_research: 关键优先事项包括剖析免疫调节机制、评估抗病毒及免疫调节疗法,以及推动疫苗和监测体系的研发。

papers.summary_zh: 背景：近期在邮轮上的安第斯病毒疫情引发全球公共卫生关注,促使对汉坦病毒的生物学和疾病进行综述。 主要方向：本综述概述了两大临床综合征(HFRS 与 HCPS),并强调病毒进入、免疫逃逸以及宿主免疫失调为核心主题。 研究现状：目前的认识指出病毒介导的细胞病变和宿主驱动的免疫病理是主要致病机制,汉坦病毒蛋白拮抗I型干扰素和自噬。 不足：病毒免疫逃逸策略与随之而来的失控宿主免疫反应之间的确切相互作用仍缺乏明确阐明。 后续研究：关键优先事项包括剖析免疫调节机制、评估抗病毒及免疫调节疗法,以及推动疫苗和监测体系的研发。

papers.title: Eleven questions on Hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome management in the ICU.
papers.abstract: Hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS) due to Andes virus (ANDV) is a fulminant yet potentially reversible cause of respiratory and circulatory failure requiring timely critical care. This article addresses eleven practical questions on ICU management, drawing on clinical experience and research from the Chilean healthcare system. The recommendations cover early recognition, diagnostic workup, haemodynamic monitoring, cautious fluid and vasoactive support, respiratory management, VA-ECMO referral, daily ICU care, recovery, common pitfalls, and therapies with limited evidence. Because no antiviral or immunomodulatory therapy has consistently improved outcomes, survival relies on early suspicion, physiology-guided supportive care, and rapid escalation to ECMO-capable centres when severe cardiopulmonary failure develops.

papers.title: Andes virus on cruise ships: An evidence-stratified review of transmission risks and biosecurity strategies.
papers.abstract: The 2026 Andes virus (ANDV) cluster associated with the merchant vessel (MV) Hondius cruise ship highlights the limitations of hantavirus control strategies that have traditionally focused on rodent-source exposure alone. No evidence supports heating, ventilation, and air conditioning (HVAC)-mediated long-distance ANDV spread. Such strategies are insufficient for ecologically sensitive cruise routes, enclosed ocean-going environments, international passenger movement, and limited onboard medical capacity. Current evidence indicates that ANDV has limited but documented potential for person-to-person transmission. Transmission is most plausibly associated with acute-phase viremia, exposure to body fluids or short-range droplets, prolonged close contact, caregiving, and specific contextual conditions; it should not be equated with sustained community transmission by highly efficient respiratory viruses. On the basis of epidemiologic investigations, clinical shedding studies, animal models, viral genetic evidence, and environmental stability data, this review analyzes how high-consequence pathogens may have their public health impact amplified in cruise-ship settings. It further proposes prevention and control measures covering pre-voyage ecological exposure assessment, embarkation screening, early onboard recognition, tiered isolation, rapid shipboard testing, medical evacuation, and cross-border coordination. The central lesson from the MV Hondius event is that cruise ships operating on ecologically sensitive routes should move beyond conventional sanitation-centered management toward a whole-of-journey biosecurity model based on evidence stratification and graded response.

papers.title_zh: 安第斯病毒 在邮轮上:基于证据分层的传播风险与生物安全策略综述。

analysis_zh.background: 2026年 安第斯病毒 集群在 MV Hondius 邮轮上显示,传统的 汉坦病毒 控制侧重于啮齿动物暴露,对海事环境而言不足。
analysis_zh.main_directions: 综述强调了传播机制(急性期病毒血症、体液、近距离飞沫、密切护理),并提出在航程中实施分层生物安全干预措施。
analysis_zh.current_state: 证据证实,安第斯病毒(ANDV)存在有限但已记录的人际传播,这与高效呼吸道病毒的持续社区传播不同。
analysis_zh.gaps: 暂无数据支持 HVAC 介导的远距离传播,导致对封闭船舶环境中空气传播风险存有不确定性。
analysis_zh.future_research: 作者呼吁实施并评估航前生态评估、船上筛查、快速检测、分层隔离以及跨境协作,以为循证分层生物安全提供依据。

papers.summary_zh: 背景：2026年 安第斯病毒 集群在 MV Hondius 邮轮上显示,传统的 汉坦病毒 控制侧重于啮齿动物暴露,对海事环境而言不足。 主要方向：综述强调了传播机制(急性期病毒血症、体液、近距离飞沫、密切护理),并提出在航程中实施分层生物安全干预措施。 研究现状：证据证实,安第斯病毒(ANDV)存在有限但已记录的人际传播,这与高效呼吸道病毒的持续社区传播不同。 不足：暂无数据支持 HVAC 介导的远距离传播,导致对封闭船舶环境中空气传播风险存有不确定性。 后续研究：作者呼吁实施并评估航前生态评估、船上筛查、快速检测、分层隔离以及跨境协作,以为循证分层生物安全提供依据。
